title: Peter Damian (21 February)
hook: a monk and reformer who wrote blunt letters against corruption in the Church

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jacinta and Francisco Marto, the children of Fatima, saints for how they lived. Your line was the children of fatima. Whose seriousness did you take seriously? Day nine hundred seventy.

Some letters you write three times. The first draft is furious. The second is so polite it says nothing. The third, if you're lucky, says the true thing plainly, because you care about the person reading it. Peter Damian spent much of his life writing the third kind. He was a monk in Italy who loved silence and his hermit's cell, and he kept being pulled out of it to tell bishops, priests and even popes what they did not want to hear. He signed himself, tradition says, Peter the sinner, monk. Today is about him, and about love that doesn't flatter.
screen: `THREE DRAFTS OF A HARD LETTER.` → `A MONK PULLED FROM HIS CELL.` → `PETER THE SINNER, MONK.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Peter Damian began poor. An orphan, he was taken in by relatives and set to work as a boy looking after pigs, until an older brother saw how bright he was and paid for his schooling. He became a teacher, then left it all for a hermitage, where the monks lived in small cells and prayed through the night. He would have stayed. But the Church of his day was sick in ways that were hard to miss. Church offices were being bought and sold, a corruption known as simony. Clergy were living double lives. Peter wrote about it, in letters that named things plainly, and the popes kept calling him to help with reform. He was made a cardinal and bishop, and, tradition says, asked more than once to be allowed to go back to his cell. What makes him worth remembering is not just that he was blunt. Plenty of people are blunt. It's that he aimed the same honesty at himself. That signature, Peter the sinner, was not a pose. The book of Proverbs, in the Douay-Rheims, has a line for this kind of friend: "Better are the wounds of a friend, than the deceitful kisses of an enemy." Peter Damian's letters could wound. He wrote them because he loved the Church, not because he wanted to win. The Church later named him a Doctor of the Church, a teacher for everyone. Blunt love tells the truth, includes itself in the problem, and stays to help fix it.
screen: `A SWINEHERD BOY, THEN A HERMIT.` · `A CHURCH SELLING ITS OFFICES.` · `BLUNT LETTERS, AND BLUNT WITH HIMSELF.` · `CALLED TO HELP, LONGING FOR HIS CELL.` · then, large: `BETTER ARE THE WOUNDS OF A FRIEND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one corruption, gently. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing that's gone a little crooked: at work, in a group you belong to, in your own habits. A rule bent for friends. A small lie that's become normal. Name it, privately, in plain words, the way Peter Damian would. Then do what he did with his signature: find your own part in it, however small. Don't plan a speech. Just see it clearly. If you pray, you can bring it to God and ask for the courage to say it kindly. If you don't, let it sit, named, while you breathe. The bell holds the time.
Peter Damian. A hermit monk and reformer, later a cardinal and Doctor of the Church, who wrote hard letters out of love and called himself Peter the sinner.
Your line: blunt love. Today, if a hard thing needs saying, say it plainly and warmly, and say your own part first. Day nine hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Catholics keep 21 February as the memorial of Saint Peter Damian, bishop and Doctor of the Church, and his letters and writings on prayer are read in the Liturgy of the Hours and by those interested in Church reform.
